result.relation_rationale: The report directly assesses the requested radiographic progression-free survival from randomization, with radiographic progression or death as events, comparing assignment to abiraterone plus SOC (with or without radiotherapy) against SOC without abiraterone. This is the overall population, but one randomized patient withdrew consent for analysis, so the analyzed population is slightly narrower than all randomized participants.

measurement.method: Soft-tissue progression assessed by CT or MRI using RECIST 1.1 and bone progression assessed by bone scan using adapted PCWG2 criteria.

time_point_or_window.description: From randomization until radiographic progression or death from any cause; participants without events were censored at last follow-up.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence random?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if a random component was used in the sequence generation process. Examples include computer-generated random numbers; reference to a random number table; coin tossing; shuffling cards or envelopes; throwing dice; or drawing lots. Answer ‘No’ if no random element was used in generating the allocation sequence or the sequence is predictable. Answer ‘No information’ if the only information about randomization methods is a statement that the study is randomized.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether a random component was used to generate the allocation sequence.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes when a random component was used; answer no when no random element was used or the sequence is predictable. A statement that the study is randomized alone supports no_information.
evidence_needed: The sequence-generation method, such as computer random numbers, a random number table, coin tossing, or minimization with a random element.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the only information about randomization methods is that the study is randomized. Do not turn missing reporting into proof that the sequence was non-random.

answer_anchors.text: A random component was used in sequence generation.
No random element was used, or the sequence was predictable.
The report only states that the study is randomized.

considerations: Minimization should generally be considered random when it includes a random element.

Sequence generation asks how the allocation sequence was produced; concealment asks whether forthcoming assignments were hidden before enrolment and assignment; baseline imbalance asks whether the resulting groups suggest a randomization problem. Evidence for one does not answer the others.
The baseline-imbalance answer must not change this answer.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the sequence method. A truncated search does not establish that the method is absent.

questions.wording: Was the allocation sequence concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned to interventions?
questions.official_guidance: Answer ‘Yes’ if the trial used any form of remote or centrally administered method to allocate interventions to participants, where the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit or organization, independent of the enrolment personnel. Answer ‘Yes’ if envelopes or drug containers were used appropriately. Answer ‘No’ if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 17, Box 4, signalling question 1.2
questions.bias_construct: Whether the allocation sequence was concealed until participants were enrolled and assigned.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes for remote or centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment personnel, or appropriately used opaque sequentially numbered sealed envelopes or identical sequentially numbered drug containers. Answer no when the enrolling investigator or participant could know the forthcoming allocation.
evidence_needed: The method used before assignment and who controlled it; for envelopes or containers, capture the details that make them tamper-resistant and irreversible before assignment.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when the report does not provide enough information to assess concealment; do not infer concealment from central registration or a sequence number alone.

answer_anchors.text: Remote or central allocation was controlled by an independent external unit, or appropriate envelopes/containers were used.
The enrolling investigator or participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation.

considerations: Allocation concealment concerns the process before assignment, not blinding after assignment.

Keep concealment separate from sequence generation (how the sequence was made) and baseline imbalance (what the randomized groups look like). A random sequence or balanced baseline table does not establish concealment.
The reported sequence-generation method does not establish concealment.
Use the returned query suggestions or wording from the report to locate the allocation safeguards. A truncated search does not establish that concealment details are absent.

questions.wording: Did baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with the randomization process?
questions.official_guidance: Note that differences that are compatible with chance do not lead to a risk of bias. Answer ‘No’ if no imbalances are apparent or if any observed imbalances are compatible with chance. Answer ‘Yes’ if there are imbalances that indicate problems with the randomization process, including substantial differences between intervention group sizes, a substantial excess in statistically significant differences beyond that expected by chance, or imbalance in one or more key prognostic factors very unlikely to be due to chance. Answer ‘No information’ when there is no useful baseline information available.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 17-18, Box 4, signalling question 1.3
questions.bias_construct: Whether baseline differences between intervention groups suggest a problem with randomization.
questions.decision_rule: Answer no when no imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance. Answer yes for substantial group-size differences, an excess of statistically significant baseline differences beyond chance, a key prognostic imbalance very unlikely due to chance and large enough to bias the estimate, or excessive similarity incompatible with chance.
evidence_needed: Baseline characteristics for the randomized groups, intended allocation ratio, prognostic factors, and outcome baseline measures.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when no useful baseline information is available, for example in an abstract or when only final-analysis participants are described.

answer_anchors.text: Baseline imbalance indicates a problem with the randomization process.
No imbalance is apparent or observed differences are compatible with chance.
No useful baseline information is available.

considerations: A few statistically significant differences at the conventional 0.05 threshold are usually compatible with chance.

This is a question about baseline imbalance suggesting a randomization problem, not about how the sequence was generated or whether allocation was concealed. Do not use the baseline table to backfill either process question.
This answer must not alter answers about sequence generation or concealment.

evidence.quote:
Between Nov 27, 2013, and Dec 20, 2018, 1173 patients
were enrolled (one patient subsequently withdrew
consent for analysis of his data) and assigned to receive
SOC (n=296), SOC plus radiotherapy (n=293), SOC plus
abiraterone (n=292), or SOC plus radiotherapy plus
abiraterone (n=291; figure 1). SOC was ADT alone in
462 patients and ADT with docetaxel in 710 patients
(table 1).

In the overall population, the addition of abiraterone to
SOC (with or without docetaxel and with or without
radiotherapy) decreased the number of radiographic
progression events or deaths from 371 to 252, improved
the median progression-free survival from 2·22 years
(IQR 1·09-6·03) to 4·46 years (1·72-not reached), and
reduced the relative risk of radiographic progression or
death by 46% compared with patients who did not receive
abiraterone (adjusted HR for radiographic progression-
free survival 0·54, 99·9% CI 0·41-0·71; p<0·0001;
figure 2A, table 2). The addition of abiraterone to SOC

Update the nature of the co-primary endpoint from PFS to radiographic PFS (rPFS): In initial protocol PFS
was based on rPFS and PSA progression events. However, post PEACE-1 initiation, various studies showed that
PSA progression had poor prognosis value as a surrogate endpoint. In contrast, rPFS was demonstrated to be a
valid surrogate endpoint for OS in metastatic prostate cancer and was an FDA-validated registration endpoint in
hormone sensitive metastatic prostate cancer settings (PEACE-1 study indication). Hence, rPFS was requalified as
a co-primary endpoint while PFS events already well defined and collected during the trial were used along with
PSA progression to characterize and evaluate CRPC-free survival as a secondary endpoint.
•
Change the distribution of the type I error between the co-primary endpoints in order to prioritize the overall
survival analysis. Thus, the type I error for OS was set at 4.9% instead of 4%, and at 0.1% instead of 1% for rPFS.

Randomisation and masking
Eligible patients were centrally randomly assigned in the
Alea Clinical Portal), in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, to SOC, SOC plus
radiotherapy, SOC plus abiraterone (abiraterone plus
prednisone), or SOC plus radiotherapy plus abiraterone.
This randomisation process was performed via the
Tenalea autonomous software, solely accessed by the trial
data manager within the Epidemioloy and Biostatistics
facility of the Gustave Roussy Center in Villejuif, France
until 2015, then by each investigator.
Randomisation was done using a minimisation
algorithm, stratified by study site, ECOG performance
status (0 vs 1-2), type of ADT (gonadotropin-releasing
hormone agonist vs antagonist vs bilateral orchiectomy),
planned administration of docetaxel (yes vs no), and
disease extent or burden based on metastatic status
(lymph node metastases only vs bone metastases [with or
without lymph node metastases] vs visceral metastases).
A similar weight was given to each of the five
stratification factors, with 80% probability to minimise
imbalance in the number of patients assigned to each
treatment group. As the case report form gathered
information for patient stratification according to
high-volume versus low-volume metastatic burden
classification (as defined in the CHAARTED study2 [high
volume was defined as the presence of visceral
metastases or at least four bone lesions with one beyond
the vertebral bodies and pelvis]), this later classification
was retained to enable inter-trial comparisons. No
masking was performed in this study.

Outcomes
The coprimary endpoints were radiographic progression-
free survival and overall survival. Radiographical pro
gression of soft-tissue lesions was evaluated by either CT
or MRI, on the basis of RECIST version 1.1. Progression
of bone lesions was assessed by bone scan according to
the adapted version of Prostate Cancer Working Group 2
criteria,21 with no secondary bone scan required to
confirm progression. Radiographic progression-free
survival was defined as the time between randomisation
and the occurrence of radiographical progression or
death from any cause. Overall survival was defined as the
time between randomisation and death from any cause.
Patients without events were censored at the date of last
follow-up.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
data.completion_rule: Ground each active proposition and its uncertainty in inspected Evidence or bounded discovery for unresolved premises. Supply every question activated by the submitted answer path with an Evidence use, scoped absence receipt, or limitation. Inactive extras are ignored.

4|Abiraterone plus prednisone added to androgen deprivation
5|therapy and docetaxel in de novo metastatic castration-
6|sensitive prostate cancer (PEACE-1): a multicentre, open-
7|label, randomised, phase 3 study with a 2 × 2 factorial design
8|Karim Fizazi, Stéphanie Foulon, Joan Carles, Guilhem Roubaud, Ray McDermott, Aude Fléchon, Bertrand Tombal, Stéphane Supiot,
9|Dominik Berthold, Philippe Ronchin, Gabriel Kacso, Gwenaëlle Gravis, Fabio Calabro, Jean-François Berdah, Ali Hasbini, Marlon Silva,
10|Antoine Thiery-Vuillemin, Igor Latorzeff, Loïc Mourey, Brigitte Laguerre, Sophie Abadie-Lacourtoisie, Etienne Martin, Claude El Kouri,
11|Anne Escande, Alvar Rosello, Nicolas Magne, Friederike Schlurmann, Frank Priou, Marie-Eve Chand-Fouche, Salvador Villà Freixa,
12|Muhammad Jamaluddin, Isabelle Rieger, Alberto Bossi, on behalf of the PEACE-1 investigators*
13|Summary
14|Background Current standard of care for metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer supplements androgen
15|deprivation therapy with either docetaxel, second-generation hormonal therapy, or radiotherapy. We aimed to
16|evaluate the efficacy and safety of abiraterone plus prednisone, with or without radiotherapy, in addition to
17|standard of care.
18|Methods We conducted an open-label, randomised, phase 3 study with a 2 × 2 factorial design (PEACE-1) at
19|77 hospitals across Belgium, France, Ireland, Italy, Romania, Spain, and Switzerland. Eligible patients were male,
20|aged 18 years or older, with histologically confirmed or cytologically confirmed de novo metastatic prostate
21|adenocarcinoma, and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1 (or 2 due to bone pain).
22|Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) to standard of care (androgen deprivation therapy alone or with
23|intravenous docetaxel 75 mg/m2 once every 3 weeks), standard of care plus radiotherapy, standard of care plus
24|abiraterone (oral 1000 mg abiraterone once daily plus oral 5 mg prednisone twice daily), or standard of care plus
25|radiotherapy plus abiraterone. Neither the investigators nor the patients were masked to treatment allocation. The
26|coprimary endpoints were radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival. Abiraterone efficacy was
27|first assessed in the overall population and then in the population who received androgen deprivation therapy
28|with docetaxel as standard of care (population of interest). This study is ongoing and is registered with
29|ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT01957436.
30|Findings Between Nov 27, 2013, and Dec 20, 2018, 1173 patients were enrolled (one patient subsequently withdrew
31|consent for analysis of his data) and assigned to receive standard of care (n=296), standard of care plus radiotherapy
32|(n=293), standard of care plus abiraterone (n=292), or standard of care plus radiotherapy plus abiraterone (n=291).
33|Median follow-up was 3·5 years (IQR 2·8-4·6) for radiographic progression-free survival and 4·4 years (3·5-5·4)
34|for overall survival. Adjusted Cox regression modelling revealed no interaction between abiraterone and
35|radiotherapy, enabling the pooled analysis of abiraterone efficacy. In the overall population, patients assigned to
36|receive abiraterone (n=583) had longer radiographic progression-free survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0·54, 99·9% CI
37|0·41-0·71; p<0·0001) and overall survival (0·82, 95·1% CI 0·69-0·98; p=0·030) than patients who did not receive
38|abiraterone (n=589). In the androgen deprivation therapy with docetaxel population (n=355 in both with
39|abiraterone and without abiraterone groups), the HRs were consistent (radiographic progression-free survival 0·50,
40|99·9% CI 0·34-0·71; p<0·0001; overall survival 0·75, 95·1% CI 0·59-0·95; p=0·017). In the androgen deprivation
41|therapy with docetaxel population, grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 217 (63%) of 347 patients who
42|received abiraterone and 181 (52%) of 350 who did not; hypertension had the largest difference in occurrence
43|(76 [22%] patients and 45 [13%], respectively). Addition of abiraterone to androgen deprivation therapy plus
44|docetaxel did not increase the rates of neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, fatigue, or neuropathy compared with
45|androgen deprivation therapy plus docetaxel alone.
46|Interpretation Combining androgen deprivation therapy, docetaxel, and abiraterone in de novo metastatic castration-
47|sensitive prostate cancer improved overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival with a modest increase
48|in toxicity, mostly hypertension. This triplet therapy could become a standard of care for these patients.

62|Introduction
63|After several decades with no substantial progress, the
64|treatment of de novo (synchronous) metastatic prostate
65|cancer has drastically evolved in the past 10 years
66|with the addition of diverse treatments to androgen
67|deprivation therapy (ADT), the former standard of care
68|(SOC). The prognosis for men with de novo metastatic
69|castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) has been
70|improved by using ADT concomitantly with either
71|docetaxel1-5 or one of the second-generation androgen
72|receptor axis inhibitors (abiraterone,6-8 apalutamide,9 or
73|enzalutamide10,11). In 2018, radiotherapy to the primary
74|tumour was also shown to extend the overall survival of
75|patients with low-volume metastatic burden.12 The
76|benefits of these various combinatory therapies were
77|confirmed by meta-analyses13-15 and have helped to shape
78|the current guidelines for the treatment of mCSPC.16-18
79|Nevertheless, it remains to be established whether
80|merging some of these new therapies could provide
81|further clinical benefits and, if so, what combination
82|might be most suitable for de novo mCSPC.19 Conducted
83|by a European consortium (PEACE),20 this study aimed to
84|evaluate the efficacy and safety of abiraterone plus
85|prednisone, with or without radiotherapy, in addition to
86|SOC (ADT with or without docetaxel).
87|Methods
88|Study design and participants
89|We conducted an open-label, randomised, active-
90|controlled, phase 3 study with a 2 × 2 factorial design
91|(PEACE-1) at 77 sites across seven European countries
92|(Belgium, France, Ireland, Italy, Romania, Spain, and
93|Switzerland). The complete list of inclusion and exclusion
94|criteria is provided in the appendix (pp 5-6). Briefly, male
95|patients aged 18 years or older with histologically confirmed
96|or cytologically confirmed prostate adenocarcinoma
97|documented as de novo metastatic by bone scan, CT, or
98|MRI (according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid
99|Tumors [RECIST] version 1.1 criteria) and an Eastern
100|Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status
101|of 0-1 (or 2 due to bone pain) were eligible for inclusion,
102|provided they had received ADT for no more than
103|3 months before randomisation and had at least 6 weeks
104|between the initiation of ADT and the first docetaxel
105|dose. Patients with a pure small-cell carcinoma, or
106|previous prostate cancer treated by a definitive local
107|treatment were not eligible. All participants provided
108|written informed consent before any study-specific
109|procedures or randomisation were initiated.
110|The initial protocol was reviewed and first approved on
111|July 10, 2013, by the French Independent Ethics
112|Committee (Comité de Protection des Personnes Ile de
113|France VII). The protocol complied with the ethical
114|principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was
115|approved by Institutional Review Boards at each study
116|site. The trial conformed with the International
117|Conference on Harmonization and Good Clinical
118|Practice guidelines, and applicable regulatory require
119|ments. Steering and Independent Data Monitoring
120|Committees roles and members are described in the
121|appendix (pp 3-4).
122|Two major protocol amendments were made during
123|the accrual period, to account for the evolution of SOC
124|for men with mCSPC. Although ADT alone was the SOC
125|when the trial began recruitment in 2013, the protocol
126|was amended on Oct 5, 2015 (273 patients had already
127|been accrued), to allow for docetaxel use in SOC
128|worldwide, after ADT with docetaxel had shown
129|improvement in overall survival.2,3 Then, in 2017, ADT
130|plus abiraterone was also shown to improve overall
131|Research in context
132|Evidence before this study
133|We searched PubMed from Jan 1, 1984, to Dec 31, 2012, for
134|papers in English, using the terms "prostate cancer",
135|"metastases", and "phase 3 trial", and found 16 studies. When
136|the PEACE-1 trial began in 2013, androgen deprivation
137|therapy (ADT) had for several decades been the standard of
138|care for men with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate
139|cancer (mCSPC). All randomised trials conducted before the
140|mid-2010s had not shown improvement in outcomes with
141|new therapies compared with ADT. During recruitment for the
142|PEACE-1 trial (2013-18), overall survival of patients with de
143|novo mCSPC was shown to be improved by combining ADT
144|with either docetaxel or one of the second-generation
145|androgen receptor axis inhibitors (abiraterone, apalutamide,
146|or enzalutamide) and radiotherapy to the primary tumour, in
147|men with low metastatic burden. It had not yet been shown
148|whether combining some of these new therapies with ADT in
149|triple therapy could provide further clinical benefits.
150|Added value of this study
151|To our knowledge, PEACE-1 is the first trial to show that
152|a triple systemic therapy-consisting of ADT, docetaxel,
153|and a second-generation androgen signalling inhibitor
154|(abiraterone, combined with prednisone)-improves both
155|radiographic progression-free survival and overall survival in
156|patients with de novo mCSPC, without excessively increasing
157|toxicity (mostly hypertension and aminotransferase increase).
158|Implications of all the available evidence
159|The findings from the PEACE-1 trial, combined with the evidence
160|from other studies, add weight to the concept that systemic
161|treatment intensification provides clinical benefit for men with
162|mCSPC and illustrate that early treatment intensification is more
163|effective than identical or similar treatments being used
164|sequentially when the disease has become castration-resistant.
165|At a minimum, patients with mCSPC with a high metastatic
166|burden who are fit enough to be treated with docetaxel should
167|be considered for this triple systemic therapy.

8|abiraterone to ADT with docetaxel (given that the
9|evaluation of ADT plus abiraterone compared with ADT
10|alone had already been addressed by other trials). Further
11|details on the amendments to the protocol and statistical
12|analysis plan are provided in the appendix (pp 7-8).
13|Evolution of the sample size and allocation of patients
14|according to these key amendments is depicted in the
15|appendix (pp 9-10).
16|Randomisation and masking
17|Eligible patients were centrally randomly assigned in the
18|Alea Clinical Portal), in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, to SOC, SOC plus
19|radiotherapy, SOC plus abiraterone (abiraterone plus
20|prednisone), or SOC plus radiotherapy plus abiraterone.
21|This randomisation process was performed via the
22|Tenalea autonomous software, solely accessed by the trial
23|data manager within the Epidemioloy and Biostatistics
24|facility of the Gustave Roussy Center in Villejuif, France
25|until 2015, then by each investigator.
26|Randomisation was done using a minimisation
27|algorithm, stratified by study site, ECOG performance
28|status (0 vs 1-2), type of ADT (gonadotropin-releasing
29|hormone agonist vs antagonist vs bilateral orchiectomy),
30|planned administration of docetaxel (yes vs no), and
31|disease extent or burden based on metastatic status
32|(lymph node metastases only vs bone metastases [with or
33|without lymph node metastases] vs visceral metastases).
34|A similar weight was given to each of the five
35|stratification factors, with 80% probability to minimise
36|imbalance in the number of patients assigned to each
37|treatment group. As the case report form gathered
38|information for patient stratification according to
39|high-volume versus low-volume metastatic burden
40|classification (as defined in the CHAARTED study2 [high
41|volume was defined as the presence of visceral
42|metastases or at least four bone lesions with one beyond
43|the vertebral bodies and pelvis]), this later classification
44|was retained to enable inter-trial comparisons. No
45|masking was performed in this study.
46|Procedures
47|In all patients in the study, ADT was planned to be
48|continuously maintained by either a gonadotropin-
49|releasing hormone agonist or antagonist, or bilateral
50|orchiectomy. Patients assigned to receive docetaxel as part
51|of SOC with continuous ADT were to receive six cycles of
52|intravenous docetaxel (75 mg/m2 per cycle; maximum
53|dose of 150 mg per cycle), to be administered every
54|3 weeks (plus or minus 3 days). Granulocyte colony-
55|stimulating factor (G-CSF) injections after each docetaxel
56|cycle were recommended until the protocol amendment
57|on Jan 22, 2018, made G-CSF prophylaxis mandatory for
58|patients who received docetaxel. The first docetaxel cycle
59|had to be administered within 14 days after randomisation
60|and be at least 6 weeks after ADT initiation. Patients
61|assigned to receive abiraterone received 1000 mg of
62|abiraterone (four 250 mg tablets, orally) once daily plus
63|prednisone 5 mg orally twice daily, starting within 6 weeks
64|after ADT initiation. PEACE-1 began accrual in 2013,
65|before the LATITUDE6 and the STAMPEDE7 abiraterone
66|trials were reported and before abiraterone was approved
67|for mCSPC, which is why we used 10 mg of prednisone,
68|similar to what is approved for metastatic castration-
69|resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Abiraterone and
70|prednisone (hereafter referred to as abiraterone) were
71|administered until disease progression to castration
72|resistance, withdrawal of consent, unacceptable toxicity,
73|or death. Patients assigned to receive radiotherapy
74|(74 Gy in 37 fractions administered over 7-8 weeks)
75|were planned to start radiotherapy at least 3 weeks
76|after docetaxel completion (but no more than 8 weeks
77|after completion). Treatments given after disease
78|progression followed common practice, and investigators
79|were able to change therapy as they thought was most
80|appropriate, on the basis of prostate-specific antigen
81|(PSA) concentration variation or clinical progression,
82|even in absence of radiographical evidence. The treatment
83|flow chart is depicted in the appendix (p 10).
84|Every enrolled patient was to be followed-up for a
85|duration of 10 years. The complete list of assessments
86|performed at each visit and follow-up intervals are
87|detailed in the appendix (pp 12-13). Survival status data
88|were gathered within 3 months of the cutoff date for
89|97% of patients.
90|Outcomes
91|The coprimary endpoints were radiographic progression-
92|free survival and overall survival. Radiographical pro
93|gression of soft-tissue lesions was evaluated by either CT
94|or MRI, on the basis of RECIST version 1.1. Progression
95|of bone lesions was assessed by bone scan according to
96|the adapted version of Prostate Cancer Working Group 2
97|criteria,21 with no secondary bone scan required to
98|confirm progression. Radiographic progression-free
99|survival was defined as the time between randomisation
100|and the occurrence of radiographical progression or
101|death from any cause. Overall survival was defined as the
102|time between randomisation and death from any cause.
103|Patients without events were censored at the date of last
104|follow-up.
105|The secondary endpoints were castration-resistant
106|prostate cancer (CRPC)-free survival, serious-genito
107|urinary-event-free survival, prostate-cancer-specific survival,
108|time to next skeletal-related event, PSA response rate,
109|prognostic study of serum PSA measured 6-8 months
110|after initiation of systemic therapy, time to pain pro
111|gression, time to chemotherapy for CRPC, quality of life,
112|changes in bone mineral density, correlation of biomarkers
113|with outcome, event rate per 100 person-years of treatment
114|analysis, and toxicity. CRPC-free survival was defined as

17|events were graded on the basis of the National Cancer
18|Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
19|Events version 4.0. Safety analysis was based on the highest
20|grade adverse event recorded during the period spanning
21|from treatment initiation to CRPC. Apart from CRPC-free
22|survival, prostate-cancer-specific survival, event rate per
23|100 person-years, and toxicity, secondary endpoint results
24|were still under investigation at the time this manuscript
25|was submitted and so are not reported here.
26|Statistical analysis
27|The initial protocol in 2013 planned for a sample size of
28|916 patients. However, due to a change in the SOC and the
29|knowledge gained from the LATITUDE and STAMPEDE
30|trial results published in late 2017, the planned sample
31|size was increased to 1173 and the coprimary study aims
32|were revised (appendix pp 7-8). Because PEACE-1 was the
33|only phase 3 trial to date that could determine abiraterone
34|efficacy in patients with mCSPC receiving ADT plus
35|docetaxel as SOC, the timing of the final analyses was
36|based on this population (population of interest). Sample
37|size calculation was performed with East software (Cytel;
38|Cambridge, MA, USA), on the basis of the assumption
39|that no significant interaction would take place between
40|radiotherapy and abiraterone, to allow for a 2 × 2 factorial
41|analysis of abiraterone efficacy. For abiraterone efficacy
42|evaluation, the predetermined acceptable probability of a
43|type I error was set at 0·05, divided between the two
44|coprimary endpoints (0·049 for overall survival and 0·001
45|for
46|radiographic
47|progression-free
48|survival).
49|We
50|hypothesised that adding abiraterone to ADT plus
51|docetaxel would improve overall survival by 30% over a
52|median of 53 months and progression-free survival by
53|40% over 30 months. Hence, with 355 patients assigned to
54|ADT with docetaxel plus abiraterone (with or without
55|radiotherapy) and 355 patients assigned to ADT with
56|docetaxel
57|without
58|abiraterone
59|(with
60|or
61|without
62|radiotherapy), 249 deaths would give an 80% power to
63|detect an overall survival hazard ratio (HR) of 0·70 at a
64|two-sided α level of 0·049. With the same group allocation,
65|262 radiographic progression events or deaths were
66|predicted to have an 80% power to detect a radiographic
67|progression-free survival HR of 0·60 at a two-sided α level
68|of 0·001.
69|This trial had a factorial design, based on the
70|assumption that there would be no interaction between
71|abiraterone and radiotherapy. Before analysing the
72|various outcomes, the presence of such an interaction
73|for both coprimary endpoints was tested by analyses of
74|maximum likelihood estimates using a Cox model
75|adjusted for stratification factors (ECOG performance
76|status [0 vs 1-2], ADT type [gonadotropin-releasing
77|hormone agonist vs antagonist vs bilateral orchiectomy],
78|metastatic burden [low vs high; as defined in the
79|Randomisation and masking section],2 and docetaxel
80|[no docetaxel before amendment vs no docetaxel after
81|amendment vs with docetaxel after amendment]). In the
82|absence of a qualitative interaction (p>0·05) between
83|abiraterone and radiotherapy, the groups were to be
84|combined two by two on the basis of abiraterone
85|administration, regardless of radiotherapy, before se
86|quentially assessing abiraterone efficacy first in the
87|overall population and then in the ADT with docetaxel
88|population (assuming the significance level was reached
89|in first instance). As the preplanned number of pro
90|gression-free survival and overall survival events had
91|not been reached in the study population at the time
92|this paper was written, the efficacy of radiotherapy
93|remains to be analysed (appendix p 16). The coprimary
94|endpoint results presented here correspond to the final
95|planned analysis; no interim analysis was conducted.
96|All efficacy analyses were conducted in the intention-to-
97|treat population, defined as all patients who were
98|randomly assigned to a treatment group. Safety analyses
99|were conducted in the safety population, according to
100|the treatment actually received by the patients (those
101|who did not receive any investigational treatment were
102|not included in the safety analyses).
103|The median follow-up was estimated by the inverse
104|Kaplan-Meier method. Time-to-event endpoints were
105|estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method. The Cox
106|proportional hazards model adjusted for radiotherapy
107|and stratification factors provided significances and an
108|estimate of the abiraterone effect (p value and HR with
109|CIs adjusted to match adjustment made to significance
110|levels in the corresponding test [ie, 99·9% for
111|radiographic progression-free survival, 95·1% for overall
112|survival, and 95% for secondary endpoints]). The
113|assumption of proportional hazards was evaluated on
114|the basis of the weighted Schoenfeld residuals. The
115|heterogeneity of the effect of abiraterone in the
116|predefined stratification subgroups was evaluated using
117|Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for radio
118|therapy and stratification factors and including an
119|interaction term between abiraterone and the studied
120|stratification variable. These analyses are illustrated
121|using forest plots. Notably, we analysed the efficacy of
122|abiraterone in the ADT with docetaxel population by
123|disease burden. Non-parametric CIs for the median
124|survival differences between groups were analysed by
125|the bootkm function of the R Hmisc package

5|relative risk of radiographic progression or death by
6|42% and 53%, in patients with low metastatic burden
7|and patients with high metastatic burden, respectively
8|(low-volume burden median not reached vs 2·7 years;
9|adjusted HR 0·58, 99·9% CI 0·29-1·15; p=0·0061;
10|high-volume burden median 4·1 years vs 1·6 years;
11|adjusted HR 0·47, 99·9% CI 0·30-0·72; p<0·0001;
12|appendix p 10, table 2). Median overall survival in
13|patients with high metastatic burden improved from
14|3·47 years with SOC without abiraterone to 5·14 years
15|when abiraterone was added, corresponding to a 28%
16|reduction in relative risk of death from any cause
17|(adjusted HR 0·72, 95·1% CI 0·55-0·95; p=0·019;
18|figure 2F, table 2). As the data were not mature, no
19|conclusive response in overall survival could be shown
20|for patients with low metastatic burden (figures 2E, 3D,
21|table 2).
22|In the ADT with docetaxel population, compared with
23|SOC without abiraterone, the addition of abiraterone
24|delayed castration resistance (median CRPC-free survival
25|1·45 years vs 3·21 years; HR 0·38, 95% CI 0·31-0·47;
26|p<0·0001; table 2, appendix p 11). Among patients in
27|the ADT with docetaxel population who developed
28|castration resistance and were alive at the data cutoff
29|date, 221 (84%) of 263 patients were subsequently
30|treated by at least one life-prolonging therapy and
31|213 (81%) of 263 by at least one next-generation
32|hormonal therapy in the SOC without abiraterone
33|groups, compared with 104 (74%) of 141 and 65 (46%)
34|of 141, respectively, in the SOC plus abiraterone groups
35|(appendix p 14). Prostate-cancer-specific survival was
36|also improved by the addition of abiraterone in the ADT
37|with docetaxel population (median 4·72 years vs not
38|reached; HR 0·69, 95% CI 0·53-0·90; p=0·0062;
39|table 2, appendix p 11).
40|Adding abiraterone to ADT with docetaxel (with or
41|without radiotherapy) had no effect on the number of
42|docetaxel cycles administered (median 6 [IQR 6-6] in
43|both groups). 138 (61%) of 226 patients in the ADT with
44|docetaxel population and 183 (53%) of 347 in the ADT
45|without docetaxel population had abiraterone treatment
46|discontinued, including 29 (21%) of 138 and 32 (17%) of
47|183 due to toxicity, respectively (appendix p 14). Overall,
48|the median abiraterone treatment duration before
49|discontinuation was 33·2 months (95% CI 25·5-43·2) in
50|the ADT without docetaxel population and 34·1 months
51|(30·0-43·5) in the ADT with docetaxel population.
52|In the ADT with docetaxel safety population, 217 (63%)
53|of 347 patients who received abiraterone versus 181 (52%)
54|of 350 who did not receive abiraterone had at least
55|one severe adverse event (grade 3 or worse) and
56|seven (2%) versus three (1%) had a fatal adverse event
57|(table 3, appendix p 14). In the ADT without docetaxel
58|population, 149 (66%) of 226 patients who received
59|abiraterone had at least one severe adverse event and
60|eight (4%) had a fatal adverse event (table 2). Therefore,
61|the addition of docetaxel to abiraterone did not increase
62|the incidence of severe or fatal adverse events. In the
63|ADT with docetaxel population, 49 severe adverse events
64|occurred per 100 person-years in patients who received
65|abiraterone compared with 55 per 100 person-years in
66|patients who did not receive abiraterone (appendix p 14).
67|The incidence of frequent severe adverse events (grade 3
68|or worse adverse events that were reported in ≥5% of
69|patients) was similar between patients who received
70|abiraterone and patients who did not in the ADT with
71|docetaxel population, except for hypertension (76 [22%]
72|of 347 patients vs 45 [13%] of 350) and hepatotoxicity with
73|increased aminotransferases (20 [6%] of 347 vs two [1%]
74|of 350), which were more frequent among those who
75|received abiraterone (table 3). Although the incidence of
76|severe hypertension and hepatotoxicity were similar in
77|patients who received abiraterone in the ADT with
78|docetaxel and ADT without docetaxel populations, there
79|was a difference, as expected, in the incidence of severe
80|neutropenia, which occurred in 34 (10%) of 347 patients
81|versus none of 226, respectively (appendix p 15).
82|Although severe fatigue and peripheral neuropathy
83|events did not reach the frequency cutoff of 5% in the
84|ADT with docetaxel population, ten (3%) of 347 patients
85|who received abiraterone and 15 (4%) of 350 who did
86|not receive abiraterone had at least one event of severe
87|fatigue, and four (1%) and six (2%) had at least one
88|severe peripheral neuropathy event (table 3).

4|Discussion
5|To our knowledge, this is the first trial to show that a
6|triple systemic therapy, consisting of ADT, docetaxel,
7|and a second-generation androgen signalling inhibitor
8|(abiraterone), extends radiographic progression-free survival
9|and overall survival in patients with de novo mCSPC.
10|Whether the systemic treatment of high-volume disease
11|(ie, extended metastatic spread) should differ from that of
12|low-volume disease has been extensively debated. The
13|benefit of ADT with docetaxel has been clearly shown for
14|patients with mCSPC with high-volume disease,4,22 but
15|data collected from larger populations support a similar
16|benefit across high-volume and low-volume disease.3 This
17|discrepancy might result from different ratios of patients
18|with de novo versus relapsing low-volume disease being
19|included in these trials, because recurrences favour better
20|prognoses.23 Second-generation androgen receptor axis
21|inhibitors have shown overall survival benefits in patients
22|with mCSPC regardless of the disease volume
23|considered.5,9,10 In this trial, the mature data for men with
24|high-volume disease indicate a clear improvement in
25|both radiographic progression-free survival and overall
26|survival when abiraterone is added to ADT with docetaxel.
27|Even though the data on overall survival were immature
28|for patients with low-volume disease, an abiraterone-
29|mediated benefit in radiographic progression-free
30|survival was already apparent. Thus, ADT with docetaxel
31|plus abiraterone should be proposed as a new SOC for
32|patients presenting with high-volume disease who are fit
33|for docetaxel prescription. However, for patients with low-
34|volume disease, the decision of whether to use two or
35|three agents should be carefully considered by both the
36|patients and their oncologists, to determine whether a
37|major benefit in radiographic progression-free survival
38|(HR 0·58) is sufficient to justify a treatment inten
39|sification in a context of immature overall survival data. It
40|would also depend on whether an overall survival benefit
41|is required. Long-term data and consensus conferences
42|will allow for clinical practice guidance refinement.
43|As abiraterone can inhibit CYP3A4 in vitro,24 and as
44|CYP3A4 is involved in docetaxel elimination,25 the
45|concomitant administration of these two drugs could
46|potentially increase docetaxel exposure and thereby its
47|toxicity. However, no increase in chemotherapy-related
48|side-effects occurred in reaction to this concomitance,
49|which might suggest an absence of substantial drug-
50|drug interactions between abiraterone and docetaxel.
51|This finding is consistent with the observation that
52|abiraterone and docetaxel have similar pharmacokinetic
53|behaviour when administered alone or in combination.26
54|Similarly, abiraterone did not affect the clearance of
55|another taxane, cabazitaxel, by CYP3A.27 We also did not
56|observe an increase in haematological toxicity when
57|abiraterone was added to ADT with docetaxel, contrary to
58|a phase 2 trial in patients with mCRPC.28 The most
59|frequent high-grade adverse event reported among
60|patients who received abiraterone in this trial was
61|hypertension (22% of patients who received abiraterone
62|vs 13% of those who did not). This expected adverse event
63|was carefully monitored and managed to prevent the
64|onset of cardiovascular events, which were not seen in
65|excess in this trial. In the ENZAMET trial,10 hypertension
66|was also two times as frequent among patients with

7|higher incidences of fatigue, syncope, and therapy
8|discontinuation were reported, whereas we did not
9|observe a rise in such events in PEACE-1 with the addition
10|of abiraterone to ADT with docetaxel. Aminotransferase
11|increase, a common side-effect of abiraterone, was
12|observed in this trial (6% of patients who received
13|abiraterone vs 1% of those who did not), but occurred at a
14|similar frequency with or without docetaxel. This
15|aminotransferase increase had no detectable clinical
16|consequences, as recommended management was
17|followed.29 Notably, the addition of abiraterone to ADT
18|with docetaxel did not affect severe neutropenia incidence
19|(10% of patients who received abiraterone vs 9% of those
20|who did not). The impact of toxicity on participants will
21|be better understood after the formal analysis of quality-
22|of-life data, at which time the triplet therapy oncological
23|benefits might still outweigh the adverse effect of the
24|additional toxicity.
25|Aside from the limitations inherently associated with
26|open-label trials, the rapid clinical practice evolution
27|for mCSPC that took place during the conduct of
28|this trial prompted the sequential amendment of the
29|PEACE-1 protocol and statistical analysis plan to reflect
30|those changes, answer meaningful questions, and
31|implement the best treatment options to all participants
32|(appendix pp 7-8). In particular, as an overall survival
33|benefit for patients with mCSPC treated with abiraterone
34|combined with ADT alone was shown in 2017, accrual was
35|then restricted to patients receiving ADT with docetaxel as
36|SOC, and our pre-established statistical analysis was
37|revised to specifically include the assessment of the
38|efficacy of abiraterone in terms of survival outcomes in
39|the ADT with docetaxel population. De facto, further
40|allocating men to ADT only would have been unethical,
41|given that the ADT plus abiraterone combination was
42|already known to improve overall survival.

44|ADT and docetaxel improves both radiographic

1|Articles 2|www.thelancet.com Vol 399 April 30, 2022 3|1705 4|with ADT and docetaxel without abiraterone. Indeed, 5|docetaxel and abiraterone have distinct mechanisms of 6|action. In addition, they do not display absolute cross- 7|resistance, as abiraterone improves overall survival 8|after docetaxel treatment and docetaxel retains some 9|activity after abiraterone failure.30,31 Collectively, these 10|observations provide a rationale for the survival benefits 11|resulting from their combination in this trial. However, 12|this study did not answer whether this triple 13|combination yields clinical advantages over ADT plus a 14|second-generation androgen receptor axis inhibitor. 15|Indeed, at the time when this trial was conducted 16|(2013-18), combining ADT with such an inhibitor had 17|not been approved for mCSPC, thereby precluding 18|such a comparison within the trial. Incidentally, the 19|ongoing phase 3 ARASENS (NCT02799602) and 20|ENZAMET (NCT02446405) trials are also testing the 21|combined efficacy of second-generation androgen 22|receptor axis inhibitors (darolutamide and enzalutamide, 23|respectively) with ADT and docetaxel, and their 24|upcoming overall survival results will put the benefits 25|of abiraterone in perspective. 26|Reaching treatment synergy and preventing acquired 27|resistance despite tumour clonal heterogeneity are 28|cardinal aspects of mCSPC management that require 29|an optimisation of the treatment framework. In 30|PEACE-1, significant survival benefits were obtained 31|when abiraterone was added to ADT with docetaxel. 32|Remarkably, these benefits were observed even though 33|more than 80% of the SOC without abiraterone group 34|eventually received a second-generation androgen 35|receptor axis inhibitor (mostly abiraterone or enzaluta 36|mide) to address cancer progression. Indeed, by contrast 37|with previous trials, PEACE-1 investigators were allowed 38|to prescribe early salvage treatments to the control 39|group patients who showed evidence of cancer 40|progression. To this end, a PSA minimum value of just 41|0·50 ng/mL was used to define mCRPC, even in the 42|absence of radiographic progression. Collectively, these 43|observations suggest that the upfront combination 44|implemented in this trial is superior to the sequential 45|administration of these (or similar) agents as occurred 46|in the control group. Of note, abiraterone is approved 47|for metastatic prostate cancer in many countries and is 48|close to becoming a worldwide generic drug. 49|In conclusion, this trial not only confirms that 50|combining abiraterone with SOC improves outcomes in 51|men with de novo mCSPC, but it shows that combining 52|abiraterone with ADT and docetaxel improves overall 53|and radiographic progression-free survival and other 54|efficacy 55|endpoints 56|with 57|little 58|toxicity 59|increase. 60|Nonetheless, as PEACE-1 only included patients with 61|de novo mCSPC, it is still unclear whether this triple 62|therapy might benefit patients with metachronous 63|mCSPC. Our findings cannot directly address whether 64|this triplet systemic combination is superior to ADT 65|and abiraterone. Longer follow-up is required to answer 66|whether combining such an intensive first line systemic 67|treatment with radiotherapy to the primary tumour 68|might provide further clinical benefits for patients with 69|mCSPC. This upcoming analysis will be performed 70|when 71|the 72|preplanned 73|number 74|of 75|radiographic 76|progression-free survival and overall survival events is 77|reached in the population of men presenting with 78|low-volume metastatic dissemination. 79|Contributors 80|KF, AB, and SF conceived and designed the study. item.aggregated_output:
# Select Evidence

Use this reference while locating Result support and answering Domain questions.

## Receipt and continuation recovery

Most MCP calls return their typed result in `structuredContent`. Keep the full
receipt, including `head`, `data`, and any `next_action`, `recovery`, or cursor.
When `structuredContent` is absent, inspect the text in `content`. If the result
is an error or a validation error, use the named schema path to correct the
argument and retry the call. A structured `outcome:"repair"` lists paths in
`repairs`; fix those paths in the complete draft and resubmit it. Increase a
host output limit only after the host reports truncation. A missing receipt is
not a no-hit result.

Context pages use `data.context_page.next_cursor`. Pass that value unchanged
until it is null. If a cursor is invalid, recapture the preceding page. If a
cursor is stale, restart the first scoped request. Read each page in a separate
host-visible output when the host can truncate a combined transcript.

Branch on the result before retrying:

- When a tool requests input or elicitation, let the host complete that interaction. Do not treat it as missing scientific data.
- When proposal approval is declined or cancelled, leave the Review pending and wait for researcher direction.
- When the host does not support elicitation, report that capability condition. Repeating the same call cannot add the capability.
- When a condition reports corrupt canonical or Source state, stop the affected operation and report the condition. Do not fabricate handles or resubmit the same request.
- When Domain context reports an oversized header, item, or page, restart the same explicit Trial and Domain scope with the returned `max_response_bytes`. Otherwise omit that argument. This is different from following a valid cursor.

## Keep returned handles distinct

The prefixes identify different values. `eh_` is a passage Evidence handle,
`sh_` is a captured Source handle, `sr_` is a search receipt handle, and
`sha256:` is a content identity. Copy each value directly from the response.
Use an `eh_` value only after inspecting the complete returned passage. If a
handle is rejected, reread or relist the exact returned object and correct every
occurrence. Never replace one prefix with another or retype an opaque value.

## Reuse inspected passage handles

`search_sources` locates candidate pages. Copy each returned `source_id` exactly
and use it with the same `trial_id`. Each `data.hits[]` item returns a
`passage_ref` for its exact displayed window. A hit is a discovery candidate,
not retained Evidence, until you inspect the complete passage and select it.
Choose short Source wording or a returned query suggestion. Use `all` for every
token on one page, `phrase` for contiguous token matching under the tokenizer,
`literal` for contiguous wording after presentation normalization without
stemming, `any` for broad discovery, and `prefix` for token prefixes.
Suggestions are alternatives, not a checklist.
To inspect further candidates, pass `next_cursor` as `cursor` with the same
query, mode, Source scope, and limit. A truncated batch is not the full ranking.
A zero-hit response states what its explicit lexical mode matched and only
establishes that the issued query matched no captured text. It does not establish
that the method or fact is absent. Compare the complete-query page count with
the per-term counts; individual terms do not imply co-occurrence or a phrase
match. For a Source-scoped miss, inspect the returned navigation entries and
read relevant pages; use the progressive `list_sources` action only when more
entries remain. Use the observed gap and wording from inspected Sources to
choose whether to reformulate or read the relevant section directly. The
`search_sources_batch` tool accepts up to eight independent requests, each with
its own mode, outcome, and continuation cursor; use it only when all query
inputs are already known, and wait for a result before choosing a dependent
reformulation. No fixed number of queries proves completeness.
Each item has its own success, condition, error, and continuation state. A
bounded aggregate may return successful items alongside an omitted or
continuable item; keep those successes and resume only the affected item with
its own cursor. Do not treat an aggregate size condition as failure of every
query or retry the complete batch blindly.
Use `term_feedback` after an unhelpful combined search to distinguish absent
query vocabulary from terms present somewhere in a Source despite no full-query
match. It reports bounded distinct matching-page counts by Source and the count
for the complete query under its mode; counts do not establish relevance,
co-occurrence, or phrase adjacency. Reformulate with inspected study wording or
inspect the likely Source section when the counts guide the next query or read.
Per-term searches remain optional.
The Domain context may expose per-Source `coverage`. Use it to distinguish an
unsearched Source, a surfaced candidate, a searched no-hit, an incomplete
retrieval, and a read/selected passage. A protocol, SAP, or supplement shown as
`unsearched` or `candidate_only` is a recovery opportunity, not evidence that a
premise was not reported. `searched_no_match` remains a lexical fact and never
supports a scientific absence claim. Render delivery records pixels only; it
does not establish visual inspection or comprehension.
`read_pages` likewise prepares a `passage_ref` for each non-empty window. After
you inspect a complete passage, reuse that handle in Proposal `passage_refs` or
Domain `bases`; no separate text-selection call is required.
If the serialized UTF-8 response bound splits one physical line, the returned
fragment includes exact character offsets and `next_start_char` but has no
`passage_ref` or selectable Evidence handle. Receive every fragment, inspect
the full line, then select text Evidence with the original page and inclusive
line bounds. For Evidence already selected, retain its original handle; do not
replace it with a fragment handle. A page-boundary continuation uses the
returned line continuation in the same way.

## Recover omitted Evidence

Use this procedure when an omitted passage needs inspection or its content is
no longer available to you.

1. Call `read_pages` with `recovery.trial_id` and `recovery.windows`.
2. If `data.remaining_windows` is nonempty, call `read_pages` with the same
   `trial_id` and `windows` set to that list. Omit `source_id`, `pages`, and
   top-level `start_line`.
3. Repeat until no windows remain. The returned lines then cover every requested
   window through its original `end_line`.
4. Inspect the complete passage before citing it.

The original Evidence handle identifies the complete passage. A partial
`passage_ref` from `read_pages` identifies only the range returned in that call.

Tool page numbers are 1-based Source indexes, not printed page labels. Read the
numbered Source text; never reconstruct PDF text from a preview. For comparison
across Sources, use independent `windows`. A passage crossing a page boundary needs one
selection on each page.

Use `select_text_evidence` after inspecting the source text when the prepared
passage needs different boundaries. Select one contiguous inclusive line range containing
the complete premise and its needed header, list, cohort, denominator, unit, or
footnote. A heading or list-introducing lead-in alone is incomplete.

## Use visual Evidence for visual meaning

Call `render_page` when layout, axes, columns, symbols, or footnotes affect the
meaning. Inspect the returned pixels, then call `select_visual_evidence` with the
`delivery_receipt` from the same response, a normalized region, and a literal,
self-contained transcription. A receipt is issued only when the response includes
an MCP `ImageContent` block; `inline=false` returns metadata without a receipt and
cannot support visual Evidence. Include every applicable title, axis, series,
label, value, unit, uncertainty, denominator, and footnote visible in the region.

The server binds the receipt to the exact Trial, Source, render, and PNG hash.
It records that it returned the image block; the receipt does not establish that a
person or model inspected or understood it. The host supplies the transcription;
`text_corroborated` means the complete-page transcription also occurs in extracted
Source text, while `host_visual` means it is grounded in the delivered pixels.
Host-visual Evidence can support only literal visible labels, endpoint text,
values, axes, arm labels, and stated timing. Use narrative or text-corroborated
Evidence for population, analysis or measurement methods, prespecification, and
conduct. Put interpretation in the Result rationale or Domain justification,
not in the transcription.

## Ground a Result

Use `passage_refs` for ordinary Result support and `applicability.evidence` for
design support. Do not place Evidence objects in `reported`. Use ordinary
selected Evidence for a single passage; use `table_multispan` only when a table
title or definition, header, quantitative row, unit, or footnote was selected
as separate passages. Give each selection its actual role and handle. Those
spans remain separate citations: do not concatenate their text, assume they
are adjacent, or claim that they scientifically belong together merely because
they are used by one Result.

Copy `reported.endpoint.name`, `reported.precision`, and other Source-owned
quantities from the quantitative passage. Include `reported.endpoint.definition`
only when one selected passage explicitly joins that name and definition.
For `analysis_population`, a supported summary may combine passages when it preserves
the reported inclusion criteria and exclusions. Caller-owned target interpretation,
timing, and arm assignments do not need duplicate source quotations.
For a categorical profile, `category_axis_names` names the ordered non-treatment
dimensions; it does not replace Evidence for source-reported category labels or
cells. Source-owned endpoint labels,
definitions, group or category labels, quantities, units, and denominators do.

For ordinary narrative, table, or figure Evidence, at least one item must contain
`reported.endpoint.name` and a complete quantitative tuple. A multi-span table
instead needs a cited header and quantitative-row span; the endpoint must occur
in its cited title/definition or header, and each tuple value must occur in one
of the cited header, row, unit, or footnote spans. `Total`, `Overall`, or a
similar aggregate label is not an endpoint name. Follow the tuple rules in
[Specify the Result](result.md).
Repair unsupported leaves with exact Source wording and better Evidence; a
support defect does not make the Result unavailable.

## Ground a Domain answer

Attach each basis to the active question it informs:

- `direct_support`: the passage states the answer premise;
- `indirect_support`: the passage establishes it through an explicit link;
- `contradiction`: the passage conflicts with the premise;
- `context`: the passage fixes scope or meaning;
- `inference`: the passage supplies facts from which you draw a stated conclusion;
- `absence`: an untruncated scoped search found no hits;
- `limitation`: an explicit unresolved premise and stopping rationale, with an
  optional current-Trial search receipt when retrieval provenance is useful.

Non-absence Evidence relationships use a selected Evidence handle, except
`limitation`, which uses an unresolved premise and a stopping rationale. A
directly read passage does not require a search receipt. An
`absence` receipt must
report `truncated:false`, `total_matches:0`, and `condition:"no_hits"`. A
positive search may support a limitation after you inspect the

# Assess randomization

Use this reference for Domain 1. The returned question cards supply the exact
wording, allowed answer values, guidance, and activation rules.

Keep three propositions separate:

1. **Sequence generation:** Was the allocation sequence random?
2. **Allocation concealment:** Was allocation concealed until participants were
   enrolled and assigned?
3. **Baseline differences:** Do observed imbalances suggest a problem with the
   randomization process rather than chance?

Sequence methods such as computer generation, random-number tables, lots, or
minimization may support the first proposition. Identify the random component;
concealing a predictable formula does not make it random.
For concealment, assess the pre-assignment mechanism and who could access the next
assignment. When reported facts support a probable judgment, state the inferred
safeguard or weakness. Preserve `no_information` when the details and trial
circumstances do not support that judgment.

For baseline differences, inspect the complete arm-specific baseline table or
list and any explanation. Different values are not automatically evidence of a
randomization problem. Missing reporting is not evidence that randomization
failed.

Select complete premises. A Methods heading, the word "randomized," or a
list-introducing sentence alone does not answer these questions.

When a randomization premise remains unresolved, use the active Source
inventory to include appendices, supplements, or combined documents that may
describe the actual sequence or concealment procedure. Search with concrete
study wording from the report. Continue a cursor, issue another bounded query,
or widen the Source scope when it could resolve the premise. Read the full
procedure before selecting Evidence. Stop when the complete premise is
supported or record the bounded information limit. Source role, an unopened
document, and a no-hit query do not establish how allocation was performed.

unknowns: The report does not spell out the exact allocation rule for the remaining 20% of assignments.

answers.justification: The registry states that consent and eligibility checks occurred before randomization, and the report describes assignment through Tenalea software. Together these support the inference that assignment was generated only after participants were enrolled. I judge concealment probably adequate, while recognizing that the report says investigators accessed the software after 2015 and does not describe whether upcoming assignments were inaccessible to them.
unknowns: The captured sources do not describe the platform safeguards or explicitly state who could view upcoming assignments after investigators began accessing the system.

counterevidence.implication: After 2015 each investigator accessed the randomization software; the report does not describe whether the investigator could foresee or access forthcoming assignments.

answers.justification: The full overall-population baseline table shows nearly equal group sizes (583 vs 589), similar age and ECOG distributions, and the key metastatic burden at 57% high in both groups. evidence.quote:
In the overall population, the addition of abiraterone to
SOC (with or without docetaxel and with or without
radiotherapy) decreased the number of radiographic
progression events or deaths from 371 to 252, improved
the median progression-free survival from 2·22 years
(IQR 1·09-6·03) to 4·46 years (1·72-not reached), and
reduced the relative risk of radiographic progression or
death by 46% compared with patients who did not receive
abiraterone (adjusted HR for radiographic progression-
free survival 0·54, 99·9% CI 0·41-0·71; p<0·0001;
figure 2A, table 2). The addition of abiraterone to SOC

Update the nature of the co-primary endpoint from PFS to radiographic PFS (rPFS): In initial protocol PFS
was based on rPFS and PSA progression events. However, post PEACE-1 initiation, various studies showed that
PSA progression had poor prognosis value as a surrogate endpoint. In contrast, rPFS was demonstrated to be a
valid surrogate endpoint for OS in metastatic prostate cancer and was an FDA-validated registration endpoint in
hormone sensitive metastatic prostate cancer settings (PEACE-1 study indication). Hence, rPFS was requalified as
a co-primary endpoint while PFS events already well defined and collected during the trial were used along with
PSA progression to characterize and evaluate CRPC-free survival as a secondary endpoint.
•
Change the distribution of the type I error between the co-primary endpoints in order to prioritize the overall
survival analysis. Thus, the type I error for OS was set at 4.9% instead of 4%, and at 0.1% instead of 1% for rPFS.

Randomisation and masking
Eligible patients were centrally randomly assigned in the
Alea Clinical Portal), in a 1:1:1:1 ratio, to SOC, SOC plus
radiotherapy, SOC plus abiraterone (abiraterone plus
prednisone), or SOC plus radiotherapy plus abiraterone.
This randomisation process was performed via the
Tenalea autonomous software, solely accessed by the trial
data manager within the Epidemioloy and Biostatistics
facility of the Gustave Roussy Center in Villejuif, France
until 2015, then by each investigator.
Randomisation was done using a minimisation
algorithm, stratified by study site, ECOG performance
status (0 vs 1-2), type of ADT (gonadotropin-releasing
hormone agonist vs antagonist vs bilateral orchiectomy),
planned administration of docetaxel (yes vs no), and
disease extent or burden based on metastatic status
(lymph node metastases only vs bone metastases [with or
without lymph node metastases] vs visceral metastases).
A similar weight was given to each of the five
stratification factors, with 80% probability to minimise
imbalance in the number of patients assigned to each
treatment group. As the case report form gathered
information for patient stratification according to
high-volume versus low-volume metastatic burden
classification (as defined in the CHAARTED study2 [high
volume was defined as the presence of visceral
metastases or at least four bone lesions with one beyond
the vertebral bodies and pelvis]), this later classification
was retained to enable inter-trial comparisons. No
masking was performed in this study.

Outcomes
The coprimary endpoints were radiographic progression-
free survival and overall survival. Radiographical pro
gression of soft-tissue lesions was evaluated by either CT
or MRI, on the basis of RECIST version 1.1. Progression
of bone lesions was assessed by bone scan according to
the adapted version of Prostate Cancer Working Group 2
criteria,21 with no secondary bone scan required to
confirm progression. Radiographic progression-free
survival was defined as the time between randomisation
and the occurrence of radiographical progression or
death from any cause. Overall survival was defined as the
time between randomisation and death from any cause.
Patients without events were censored at the date of last
follow-up.

item.aggregated_output:
# Assess deviations from intended interventions

Use this reference for Domain 2, which assesses the effect of assignment to
intervention. The returned question cards are authoritative.

For active conduct questions, build the chain in order:

1. What intervention was intended in each randomized group?
2. What change, non-adherence, or additional intervention occurred?
3. Did the trial context cause that change?
4. Could it affect the outcome, and was it balanced between groups?

For 2.3, a negative answer covers no relevant deviation as well as changes that
were protocol-consistent or could occur outside the trial context. An affirmative
answer needs evidence or strong reason linking a protocol-inconsistent deviation
to the trial context. State that link when it is an inference.
Do not treat subsequent treatment after progression, rescue treatment, or
cross-over as a 2.3 deviation merely because its use differed between randomized
groups or could affect the outcome. For the effect of assignment, first establish
that the subsequent treatment was prohibited or otherwise inconsistent with the
trial protocol and that the trial context caused it. Protocol-permitted subsequent
care, including ordinary treatment after progression, supports `no` or
`probably_no` for 2.3.
A protocol establishes the plan, not conduct. Different assigned treatments or
visible schedules do not by themselves prove that participants or carers knew
the assignment.

For 2.6, assess the analysis separately. Compare randomized assignment with the analyzed
population, exclusions, reassignment, and reasons. An ITT label is not proof
that all randomized participants were analyzed as assigned. Excluding only
participants with missing outcome data is not automatically the same as an
inappropriate assignment-effect analysis; keep that issue distinct for Domain
3. If an analysis defect activates the impact question, consider outcome rarity
and prognostic exclusions as well as the percentage affected.

Support each conduct-chain proposition with source facts and any stated
inference. A passage supporting one proposition does not settle the others.

## Paired premise check

Use the comparison card's neutral pair as a reasoning control. In the permitted
care case, rescue or crossover is allowed by the protocol and is ordinary later
care; in the changed case, the same treatment change is prohibited and caused
by trial participation or trial staff. Change the reasoning only when both
protocol inconsistency and a trial-context cause change. Do not import an
expected answer or risk label from the pair.

2.2
Missing data

For rPFS and OS, missing values on the outcome were handled by means of censoring. Notably, recent vital status data
(obtained within 3 months of the cut-off date) were available for 97% of the study patients. All the efficacy analyses were
done on the 1172 patients from the ITT population, except the Cox model analysis used for the rPFS analysis (there were 6
patients with missing data for the stratification factor "Disease burden", hence discarded from the analysis). These 6 missing
data were recovered at time of OS analysis so that the Cox model applied to this analysis took into account the whole study
ITT population (n=1172).

answers.justification: The article explicitly states that patients were not masked to treatment allocation in this open-label trial.
The same passage explicitly states that investigators were not masked to treatment allocation; investigators delivered or managed study interventions.

The report says treatment changes after disease progression followed common practice and investigators could adjust therapy based on PSA or clinical progression. This describes permitted subsequent care rather than a change caused by open-label trial participation that was inconsistent with protocol. The report does not identify a separate trial-context-caused deviation for this outcome.
unknowns: Arm-specific pre-progression non-adherence or other protocol-inconsistent changes are not described in the passages inspected.

answers.justification: Although the article labels the analysis intention-to-treat, the supplement states that six randomized participants with missing baseline disease-burden data were discarded from the rPFS Cox model. One additional randomized participant withdrew consent for analysis. The reported HR therefore does not include all randomized participants as assigned; the ITT label does not remove these explicit exclusions.
unknowns: No sensitivity estimate including the six participants with missing disease-burden data is reported.

counterevidence.implication: The article describes the efficacy analysis as intention-to-treat, but the supplement gives a specific exception for the rPFS Cox model and identifies six exclusions.

answers.justification: At most seven participants were omitted from the randomized efficacy population of 1173 (one consent withdrawal plus six missing disease-burden values), about 0.6%; the report observed 623 rPFS events in the compared groups (371 and 252). Given the very small exclusion count relative to the sample and event count, these exclusions are unlikely to substantially change the estimate, although their outcome experience is unavailable.
unknowns: The excluded participants' prognoses and a sensitivity analysis including them are not reported.

questions.official_guidance: If participants are aware of their assigned intervention it is more likely that health-related behaviours will differ between the intervention groups. Blinding participants, most commonly through use of a placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences. If participants experienced side effects or toxicities that they knew to be specific to one of the interventions, answer this question ‘Yes’ or ‘Probably yes’.

questions.bias_construct: Whether participants were aware of their assigned intervention during the trial.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when participants knew their assignment, including when intervention-specific side effects or toxicities revealed it. Blinding participants, commonly with placebo or sham intervention, may prevent such differences.
evidence_needed: A direct report of participant blinding, open-label conduct, or participant knowledge during the trial.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information only after considering direct facts, indirect evidence, and trial circumstances; an absent explicit awareness statement alone is insufficient when those facts support a probable judgment.

answer_anchors.text: Participants were aware of their assigned intervention.
Participants were blinded to their assigned intervention.

considerations: Awareness is about knowledge of assignment, not whether participants completed or received treatment.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.
Stratification does not prove allocation concealment.
